_changelog: v1.0.1 (2026-10-16) warn option's part 2: November's failed exercise now says the run went back to the main system and was signed with the main key in time for the cut-off, so the real pay is not left unexplained
title: The Drill
setting: a payroll bureau's Thursday night run

post.author: u/thursday_run_edvarda
post.title: Our continuity plan has passed its test four years running. Tonight it failed at step 4 in six minutes, and 12,000 people will be paid on Monday, not Friday.

blocks.text: I'm Edvarda, night operator at Brinkwell Payroll. We pay 12,000 people at 40 client firms every Friday. Each Thursday night our payroll system (one program and its records) builds a payment file for the bank, which must have it by 05:30: its cut-off for that day's payments.

The bank pays only a signed file. Signing takes three steps: our computer makes a short code from the file; a secret key, a long number, turns the code into a signature; the bank checks it with a matching number we gave it. Change one penny and it fails.

Our main key sits in a locked box inside the main system. The backup key is on a token, a small hardware stick, in a safe at our second site: a spare computer room in Ormsgill, 30 km away. The token signs only after its holder types a PIN (personal identification number). Three wrong tries lock it.

Ranulf, our manager, owns our continuity plan: the written steps for keeping pay going when the main system dies. Each March he runs a tabletop exercise: he reads out a pretend disaster, we each say what we'd do, someone notes what went wrong. Nothing is switched on. It has passed every March since 2023. The front page says "Plan tested 12 March: PASS".

For "main system down" it has four steps: declare it and call Ranulf; start our payroll system at Ormsgill; load last night's copy (our backup) and rerun the pay; sign the file with the backup key and send it. It names two key holders: J. Kisember, and our founder, who retired in 2022 and returned his token.
Our Monday test file, pretend payments the bank checks but never pays, is signed with the main key. No exercise had ever used the backup key.

After each tabletop, an after-action review lists what to fix. Each fix is a review item, one row in a spreadsheet. This row is from Thursday 20 March 2025, 19 months ago; its columns are number, date, text, owner, status:
R-7   20 Mar 2025   only one active key holder, J. Kisember; add a second   owner: (blank)   open
Kisember left on Friday 29 August 2025. He chose the PIN himself and told nobody, as the bank's rules require. This March's tabletop still passed: at step 4 someone said "the key holder signs".
Tonight, Thursday 15 October, at 01:20, the storage alarm on my run screen went red: "main storage fault, run stopped". Each line: start, step, result:

01:20  step 1  declare, call Ranulf     done 01:35
01:35  step 2  start at Ormsgill        done 02:20
02:20  step 3  load copy, rerun pay      done 03:10
03:10  step 4  sign, backup key          failed 03:16
By 03:10 the file held 12,000 payments. The Ormsgill guard opened the safe; the token asked for its PIN. I rang Kisember's number in the plan.

The main key's box is in the dead system. Enrolling a new key holder takes the bank four weeks. The cut-off passed at 05:30. The bank's rules say a late file waits for its next processing day: Monday 19 October.

blocks.label: run_night_0120_0530.png

diagram.aria: Friday 16 October 2026, 01:20 to 05:30. Step 1 runs 01:20 to 01:35, step 2 01:35 to 02:20, step 3 02:20 to 03:10, each done. Step 4 starts at 03:10 and fails at 03:16, when Kisember's number plays the disconnected tone. From 03:16 the bank file of 12,000 payments sits unsigned until the 05:30 cut-off passes.

blocks.caption: Redrawn from the run screen and my call log, Friday 16 October 2026. Green: a step done. Red: step 4, six minutes from the open safe at 03:10 to the disconnected tone at 03:16. After that the file of 12,000 payments sat unsigned at Ormsgill until the cut-off at 05:30.

blocks.text: Every step in my building worked. The one that failed sat in a safe 30 km away, under a row with no name beside it. What should we change?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Two things I'd look up before anyone answers. First, the after-action review from this March: did R-7 come up again, and what did its row say then? Second, the tabletop reports: against each of the four steps, does it say "done" or "discussed"? NIST, the US standards institute, writes in its contingency guide that a tabletop exercise "does not involve deploying equipment or other resources".

replies.author: u/thursday_run_edvarda
replies.text: The 2026 review copied R-7 forward: open, 12 months old, owner still blank. Both reports say "discussed" against all four steps.

comments.author: u/four_passes_pankraz
comments.text: Four years of PASS means the plan works. One man leaving is a staffing gap, not a broken plan. Next March get more people round the tabletop: the payroll leads, the Ormsgill guards, someone from the bank. More eyes on each step, more gaps found, and you'll catch the rest.

comments.author: u/do_it_for_real_kunibert
comments.text: Talking proves nothing. Run a full-scale exercise: every step for real, at the real second site, with a real Thursday file to the bank, as if the main system had died. Do it every month and nothing stays hidden for more than four weeks.

replies.author: u/thursday_run_edvarda
replies.text: Ranulf says a full-scale means moving a real Thursday run to Ormsgill, with 8 of us there for about 10 hours.

comments.author: u/spreadsheets_rot_adalbert
comments.text: Spreadsheets are where review items go to die. Buy continuity software: a program built to hold the plan, its contacts and every review item, and to send reminders. R-7 would never have sat there for 19 months.

reply.prompt: Ranulf wants one change agreed before next Thursday's run. What should Brinkwell change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Give each review item an owner and a date, and really sign a test file with the key.
options.part2: On Monday 19 October Ranulf went through the spreadsheet and gave every open row an owner and a due date. R-7 became his, due Friday 20 November 2026. He asked the bank that morning, and on Monday 16 November Aldegonde, our payroll team lead, was enrolled as a key holder. The plan went up a version, with her name where Kisember's had been. For four Thursdays we ran with no backup key, and the main system held. On Thursday 10 December, instead of talking step 4 through, three of us drove to Ormsgill, Aldegonde typed her PIN, and the bank's test address accepted a test file signed with the backup key. In the sim, give items an owner and a due date and choose a functional exercise each March: the owned R-7 adds Aldegonde on Monday 30 June 2025, two months before Kisember leaves, and the 12 March 2026 exercise really signs a test file and takes Kisember's dead number off the plan. Tonight's file goes at 04:00. Add the quarterly check and his number comes off on Tuesday 30 September 2025 instead.
options.senior: A review item without an owner and a date is a wish: everyone agrees with it and nobody does it. Give every item a named owner and a due date, and close it only when the plan's version has changed and the next exercise has checked it. Then make exercises climb: a tabletop finds gaps in what people know, a functional exercise really does one step, such as signing a test file with the backup key at the second site, and a full-scale exercise does everything for real. Check contacts and key holders every quarter too, because people leave between exercises.

options.text: Buy continuity software to hold the plan, its contacts and every review item.
options.verdict: The same row, in a nicer place
options.part2: In November Brinkwell bought continuity software. Every row of the spreadsheet moved across, and R-7 came with its owner field blank, because nobody had ever filled it in. The software emails each item's owner a week before its due date; rows with no owner and no date get nothing, and most of ours had neither. Aldegonde was enrolled in November because Ranulf rang the bank himself the morning after; nobody wrote that down as an item, so nothing checks that her token works. By March the software's screens looked tidy, the tabletop passed, and the front page said PASS again. In the sim, turn on continuity software: R-7 moves into it in May 2025 with no owner, Kisember still leaves on Friday 29 August 2025, and tonight still fails at 03:16.
options.senior: Software can hold a plan, but it can't own one. The tool reminds owners, and the item that broke tonight had none, so moving it changed its address, not its fate. What was missing was a person with a date and an exercise that touched the token. Tools help once owners and dates exist: they show overdue items and keep versions. Bought first, they put the same ownerless rows on a nicer screen.

options.text: Run a full-scale exercise every month, with the real second site and a real bank file.
options.verdict: Trade-off: finds it, at a price every month
options.part2: From November, on the second Thursday of each month, the real run moved to Ormsgill, 8 of us there for about 10 hours, 80 staff-hours a night. November's, on the 12th, stopped at step 4 again: Aldegonde's enrolment was four days away, so the run went back to the main system and was signed with the main key, in time for the cut-off. December's went through all four steps and she signed the real file. So did January's. By March people were swapping shifts to miss exercise nights, the same three volunteers did them all, and every exercise night put the real Friday pay on the second site for no reason but practice. In April Ranulf cut it back. In the sim, turn on the monthly full-scale: the Thursday 11 September 2025 exercise fails at step 4 and Aldegonde is enrolled on Thursday 9 October 2025, 41 days after Kisember left, so tonight's file goes at 04:00. But exercises cost 960 staff-hours a year and move 12 real runs to Ormsgill.
options.senior: A monthly full-scale exercise finds almost everything, because it does everything for real. It also spends a whole night of staff each month, moves the real run to the second site twelve times a year, and wears people out, so exercises get skipped or rushed. Full-scale is the top of the ladder, worth doing perhaps once a year for what matters most. In between, a quarterly check of contacts and key holders and a functional exercise of the riskiest step find the same gaps for far less.

options.text: Repeat the yearly tabletop with more people round the table, so more gaps come out.
options.verdict: More talk, the same untouched token
options.part2: Aldegonde was enrolled in November after Ranulf rang the bank. On Thursday 11 March 2027, 16 people sat round the table all afternoon: payroll leads, two Ormsgill guards and a visitor from the bank. At step 4 Aldegonde said she would drive to Ormsgill and sign, and the bank's visitor nodded. PASS. Nobody went. Her token had come by post to our main office in November and was still in Ranulf's desk drawer, 30 km from the safe. In the sim, turn on more people round the tabletop: both tabletops pass with 16 people, steps really run: none, 48 staff-hours a year, and tonight still fails at 03:16.
options.senior: More people round a table find more gaps in what people know and say, and none in what nobody has done. The talk at step 4 always sounds right: the key holder signs. Only signing touches the token, its PIN and where it really is. A tabletop is a good first rung, cheap and useful for roles and calls, but it must lead to a functional exercise of the step that has never been done, and its review items need owners.

sim.title: Replay Brinkwell's plan, March 2025 to tonight
sim.lede: You're Edvarda, replaying 20 months of Brinkwell's continuity plan and then the night of Thursday 15 October 2026. As given data: the plan starts at version 4 with one active key holder, J. Kisember, who leaves on Friday 29 August 2025. The exercise falls on the second Thursday of March, and the after-action review a week later raises R-7. With an owner and a due date, R-7 is Ranulf's, due Monday 30 June 2025, and Aldegonde is enrolled that day. A real step 4 that finds no PIN, or a quarterly check (on the last day of each quarter) that finds a departed holder, goes to Ranulf, the plan's owner: he takes the holder off the plan and asks the bank for a new one, which takes four weeks. A tabletop really runs no step. The monthly full-scale falls on each second Thursday. Tonight: steps 1 to 3 end at 01:35, 02:20 and 03:10; each departed holder called costs 6 minutes; an active holder drives 40 minutes to Ormsgill and takes 10 at the token. Costs a year: tabletop 8 people for 3 hours (24 staff-hours; 16 people, 48), functional 3 people for 4 hours (12), full-scale 8 people for 10 hours (80, and the real run moves to Ormsgill), monthly full-scale 960, quarterly check 8.
sim.tryThis: Try this: play to tonight as built: tabletops pass in March 2025 and March 2026, R-7 sits 19 months with no owner, and step 4 fails at 03:16. Give items an owner and a due date: Aldegonde arrives on 30 June 2025, and tonight's file goes at 04:06 after one dead number. Choose a functional exercise: it fails step 4 on 12 March 2026 and finds the gap then. Turn on the quarterly check: it finds Kisember gone on 30 September 2025. Try the monthly full-scale and watch the staff-hours, then continuity software, and 16 people round the tabletop.

explain.oneLine: Nothing in the plan's four steps was wrong, and every tabletop passed because talking never touches a token. The item that would have saved tonight, "add a second key holder", sat 19 months in a spreadsheet with no owner; Kisember left 14 months ago with the PIN, and step 4 failed at 03:16 in front of the safe at Ormsgill.

steps.title: The four steps, and the one that was only ever said.
steps.text: The plan for "main system down" runs in order. First, declare it and call the plan's owner, Ranulf: 01:20 to 01:35. Second, start the payroll system at the second site: done at 02:20. Third, load last night's copy and rerun the pay: done at 03:10, with 12,000 payments built. Fourth, sign the file and send it: the guard opens the safe, the key holder types the token's PIN, the token turns the file's short code into a signature, and the file goes to the bank. Step 4 had only ever been said aloud at a table. What could go wrong at it was everything outside the room: whether the token was there, whether anyone knew its PIN, whether its holder still worked here. Without a signature the bank pays nothing, and after its 05:30 cut-off a file waits for the next processing day, Monday. This case builds on s6e17, The Night the Lights Went Out, which chose the order to recover in; here the order was fine and the plan itself had gone stale. As s6e10, When the Building Burns, showed for backups, a step you have never really done is a hope, not a plan.

steps.title: A review item with no owner is a wish.
steps.text: The lessons-learned loop has four steps, and Brinkwell did only the first. First, the after-action review lists what went wrong: R-7, "add a second", on Thursday 20 March 2025. Second, every item gets a named owner and a due date; R-7 got neither, so it was everyone's and nobody's. Third, the owner's fix changes the plan and the plan's version goes up, so anyone can see it changed: Brinkwell's stayed at version 4 for 19 months. Fourth, the next exercise checks the change: the 2026 review simply copied R-7 forward. What goes wrong at each step: a review that lists nothing, an owner with no date, a fix that never reaches the plan, an exercise that never looks. In the sim, an owner and a due date of Monday 30 June 2025 bring Aldegonde in two months before Kisember leaves, and there is never a day without an active key holder.

steps.title: Exercises climb: talk, one step for real, everything for real.
steps.text: A tabletop is people talking a scenario through: cheap, good for roles and phone calls, and blind to equipment, because nothing is switched on. A functional exercise really does one part in a pretend setting: here, three people drive to Ormsgill, the key holder types the PIN, and a test file signed with the backup key goes to the bank's test address. A full-scale exercise runs every step for real, with a real Thursday file from the second site. Each rung proves more and costs more: 24 staff-hours a year for the tabletop, 12 for a functional exercise, 80 for a full-scale, and a full-scale every month costs 960 a year and moves 12 real runs to Ormsgill. On Thursday 12 March 2026 a functional exercise would have failed at step 4 and found the missing PIN seven months before tonight. Writing a longer plan would not have found it: more pages of steps that are only ever read aloud.

steps.title: Keep the plan current: owners, review dates and quarterly checks.
steps.text: Every plan needs an owner and a review date, and some parts go stale faster than any yearly exercise. NIST's guide says contact lists need more frequent reviews than the rest of the plan. A quarterly check is a short process. First, call every contact and key holder in the plan. Second, confirm each still works here, still answers that number and still knows their part, a PIN included. Third, take anyone gone off the plan and raise an item, with an owner and a date, for their replacement. Fourth, raise the plan's version. What can go wrong: a check that only reads the list instead of calling it. Brinkwell's check on Tuesday 30 September 2025 would have heard Kisember's dead number a month after he left, and with the bank's four weeks Aldegonde would have been enrolled by Tuesday 28 October 2025. Continuity software can hold the list and send reminders, but only to owners who exist.

steps.title: The walk to the safe at Ormsgill.
steps.text: Everything in Edvarda's building worked: the alarm, the calls, the second site's machines, the 12,000 payments built by 03:10. The cause was in the other building, where the backup key should have been ready. On Tuesday she drove the 30 km to Ormsgill with Ranulf. The guard unlocked the same safe. On its shelf sat a small envelope with "J. Kisember" written on it in his hand, and the token inside, never once used. Taped inside the safe's door was the key holder list from version 4: two names, one crossed out in 2022, and one whose number no longer rang.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn as a loop. The after-action review gives R-7 an owner, Ranulf, due Monday 30 June 2025. The fix changes the continuity plan: a new version with two key holders, Aldegonde added. The next exercise, a functional one, checks it by signing a test file with the backup key at Ormsgill. Below: each quarter, contacts and key holders are called, which feeds the plan; exercises climb from tabletop to functional to full-scale, which feeds the next exercise.

nodes.label: Each quarter: call contacts, key holders

explain.caption: The fix, drawn as a loop. Every review item gets an owner and a due date; the fix changes the plan and raises its version; the next exercise checks it, here by really signing a test file with the backup key at Ormsgill. Each quarter someone calls every contact and key holder, and exercises climb from tabletop to functional to full-scale. In the sim: Aldegonde enrolled on 30 June 2025, no day without a key holder, tonight's file at 04:00.

fix.title: The fix: an owner and a date for every item, an exercise that really signs, and quarterly checks
fix.text: Run continuity as a program, not a document. Every plan has an owner and a review date. Every after-action item gets a named owner and a due date, and is closed only when the plan's version has changed and the next exercise has checked the change. Contacts and key holders are called every quarter, and anyone gone comes off the plan the same day, with an item to replace them. Exercises climb: a tabletop for roles and calls, a functional exercise each year for the step most likely to fail, here signing a test file with the backup key at Ormsgill, and a full-scale when the stakes justify a night. For Brinkwell, the first items are R-7 (a second key holder, owned by Ranulf) and a functional exercise of step 4 within weeks, not next March.

limits: A functional exercise proves only the step it really runs: signing a test file shows the token and the PIN work, not that the second site can rebuild 12,000 payments by 03:10. Rotate which step is really run.
Owners and dates make items move, not move well: an owner can close an item on paper. Close an item only when the plan's version has changed and an exercise has checked it.
A quarterly check finds people who have left, not knowledge that has faded: a holder can answer the phone and have forgotten the PIN. Have holders really sign a test file now and then.

explain.seniorTake: A continuity plan is not a document; it is a program that keeps the document true. That means an owner and a review date for every plan, an owner and a due date for every lesson learned, a version that changes when the plan does, contacts and key holders checked every quarter, and exercises that climb from talking to doing, each one checking last time's fixes. The record to distrust is a row of PASSes from exercises that never touched the thing that would fail: a pass only proves what the exercise really ran. Staff work here is walking into the other building, the second site, the safe, the token, and asking when anyone last used it.

realWorld.title: NIST SP 800-34: lessons learned update the plan
realWorld.text: NIST's Contingency Planning Guide says: "For each TT&E activity conducted, results are documented in an after-action report, and Lessons Learned corrective actions are captured for updating information in the ISCP." TT&E is its short form for test, training and exercise; the ISCP is the system's contingency plan.

realWorld.title: NIST SP 800-34: contact lists go stale first
realWorld.text: "As a general rule, the plan should be reviewed for accuracy and completeness at an organization-defined frequency or whenever significant changes occur to any element of the plan. Certain elements, such as contact lists, will require more frequent reviews."

realWorld.title: NIST SP 800-34: from talk to full-scale
realWorld.text: "A tabletop exercise is discussion-based only and does not involve deploying equipment or other resources." And: "Functional exercises vary in complexity and scope, from validating specific aspects of a plan to full-scale exercises that address all plan elements." For high-impact systems: "The full-scale functional exercise should include a system failover to the alternate location."

realWorld.title: NIST SP 800-34: version control
realWorld.text: "Strict version control must be maintained by requesting old plans or plan pages to be returned to the ISCP Coordinator in exchange for the new plan or plan pages." In the guide, the ISCP Coordinator plays the part Ranulf plays at Brinkwell: the plan's owner.

realWorld.title: NIST SP 800-84: action items after the report
realWorld.text: The exercise guide says: "Following the development of the after action report, the plan coordinator might assign action items to select personnel in an effort to update the IT plan being exercised." A footnote names the top rung: "A comprehensive exercise of an entire IT plan is sometimes known as a full-scale exercise."

realWorld.title: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 A.5.29: security during disruption
realWorld.text: ISMS.online's summary gives the control's title as "Information Security During Disruption" and says: "In order to ensure business continuity, organisations must identify their requirements for information security." A summary page, not the standard's own text, which is paid.

realWorld.title: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 A.5.30: ICT readiness
realWorld.text: ISMS.online's summary gives the title as "ICT Readiness for Business Continuity" and says: "Regular testing and evaluation and senior management approval are essential components of ICT continuity plans."

realWorld.title: SOC 2 A1.1: capacity
realWorld.text: The first availability criterion begins: "The entity maintains, monitors, and evaluates current processing capacity and use of system components". It is about having enough capacity; continuity starts with A1.2.

realWorld.title: SOC 2 A1.2: recovery infrastructure
realWorld.text: A1.2 begins "The entity authorizes, designs, develops or acquires, implements, operates, approves, maintains, and monitors" environmental protections, software, backups and "recovery infrastructure to meet its objectives." A safe holding a token nobody can use is recovery infrastructure that is not maintained.

realWorld.title: SOC 2 A1.3: test the recovery plan
realWorld.text: "The entity tests recovery plan procedures supporting system recovery to meet its objectives." Four tabletops that never signed a file are the gap this criterion looks for.

asked: How would you run a continuity program for a company?
Tabletop, functional, full-scale: what does each prove?
How do you make lessons from an exercise change the plan?
interview.answer: I'd run continuity as a program, not a document. Every plan has a named owner and a review date, and its contacts and key holders are called every quarter, because people leave between exercises. Exercises climb a ladder. A tabletop, people talking a scenario through, proves people know their roles and the plan reads sensibly; it proves nothing about equipment. A functional exercise really does one part in a pretend setting, such as signing a test file with the backup key at the second site; it proves that step works with today's people and kit. A full-scale exercise runs everything for real, like a failover to the second site with a real run; it proves the whole chain, at the cost of a night and real risk, so I'd do it rarely and for what matters most. After every exercise an after-action review lists what went wrong; each item gets an owner and a due date, the fix changes the plan and raises its version, and the next exercise checks that fix. I'd watch two numbers: items open past their date, and steps never really run. I'd tell the story of a payroll bureau whose plan passed four tabletops while its only backup key holder had left, so the night it was needed, 12,000 people were paid three days late.

terms.def: A company that works out and pays other firms' wages for them. Brinkwell pays 12,000 people at 40 client firms every Friday.
The payroll bureau in this story. Its main system runs the Thursday night run; its second site is in Ormsgill, 30 km away.
The person who watches the overnight run and acts when it stops. Edvarda's job.
One program with its own stored records, such as the payroll system (The Night the Lights Went Out).
The one file the payroll run builds each Thursday: every person's pay, for the bank to pay out. Tonight's held 12,000 payments.
The last moment the bank takes files for that day's payments: 05:30. A file after it waits for the next processing day.
A day the bank runs payments. In this story Saturday and Sunday are not, so a file that misses Friday's cut-off is paid on Monday.
Proving a file came from you, unchanged, in steps: work out a short code from the whole file, turn it into a signature with a secret key, and let the receiver check it with the key's public half.
A stamp made with a secret key that anyone holding the matching public half can check. It proves who signed and that nothing changed since.
The secret number used to sign. Brinkwell has two that the bank accepts: the main key in a locked box in the main system, and the backup key on a token.
Brinkwell's everyday signing key, kept in a locked box wired into the main system. When the main system is down, it is down too.
The second signing key the bank accepts, held on a token in the safe at Ormsgill, for nights when the main system is down.
A small hardware stick holding a signing key. It signs only after its holder types the PIN, and locks for good after three wrong tries.
Short for personal identification number: a short secret that unlocks the token. Each holder chooses their own and tells nobody, by the bank's rules.
A person the bank has enrolled to use the backup key, who knows its PIN. Brinkwell's plan named two; only J. Kisember was active.
The bank's process for adding a key holder: Brinkwell asks, the bank checks the person and issues them access to the token. It takes four weeks.
A spare computer room somewhere else that receives copies and can run the systems if the main one dies (The Night the Lights Went Out). Brinkwell's is in Ormsgill.
The town 30 km from Brinkwell where its second site, and the safe with the backup token, sit.
A saved copy of the records, kept so they can be put back (When the Building Burns). Step 3 loads last night's copy at Ormsgill.
The written steps for keeping important work going when a system dies, in order, with who does what. Brinkwell's is owned by Ranulf.
The one person answerable for a plan: keeping it true, running its exercises and chasing its items. Ranulf owns Brinkwell's.
A number that goes up each time the plan changes, so anyone can see which copy is current. Brinkwell's stayed at version 4 for 19 months.
A rehearsal of the plan, in steps: pick a scenario, run it (by talk or for real), note what went wrong, then hold an after-action review.
A rehearsal where people round a table talk through the plan as a scenario unfolds. Nothing is switched on (The Night the Lights Went Out).
A rehearsal that really does one part of the plan in a pretend setting, such as signing a test file with the backup key at the second site.
A rehearsal of every step for real: here, the real Thursday run moved to the second site and a real file sent to the bank. It costs a night of staff.
A meeting after an exercise or a real event that lists what went wrong and what to fix. Its written result is an after-action report.
One thing to fix from an after-action review, like one row on a to-do list. It needs a named owner and a due date, or it waits.
Brinkwell's review item from Thursday 20 March 2025: "only one active key holder, J. Kisember; add a second". No owner, no due date.
The date by which a review item's owner must have fixed it.
The steps that turn an exercise into a better plan: list items, give each an owner and a due date, change the plan and its version, check it in the next exercise.
A file of pretend payments sent to the bank's test address: the bank checks its signature but never pays it.
A program built to hold plans, contacts and review items and to send owners reminders.
Calling every contact and key holder in the plan every three months to confirm each still works there, answers and knows their part.
People times hours: 8 people for 10 hours is 80 staff-hours. Used here to compare what each kind of exercise costs.
A failure of the disks where the main system keeps its records. Tonight's stopped the run at 01:20.
Brinkwell's operations manager and the continuity plan's owner.
Brinkwell's payroll team lead, enrolled as a key holder after this night (in the sim, earlier, by each fix).

atWork: An after-action item with no owner is a common pattern: a review lists the right fix, nobody's name goes beside it, and the next exercise passes because it never touches the thing the item was about. Find your continuity or disaster recovery plans and check five things. Does each plan have a named owner and a review date? Does every open review item have an owner and a due date, and how old is the oldest? When an item closes, does the plan's version change, and does the next exercise check it? When were contacts and key holders last called, rather than read? And which steps have only ever been talked through: signing with a backup key, restoring at the second site, failing over a region? On AWS, the same questions apply to the cross-region recovery runbooks and to whoever holds the emergency access they depend on. Standards, stated conditionally and not as legal advice: if your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, an auditor checking A.5.30 (ICT, short for information and communication technology, readiness for business continuity) would look for continuity plans that have been exercised and actions from those exercises that were closed, and A.5.29 covers keeping information security in place during a disruption; if it is pursuing SOC 2, criteria A1.2 and A1.3 cover recovery infrastructure and testing the recovery plan. NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 and SP 800-84 describe how to run the exercises. Dated exercise reports, an item list with owners and due dates, and a plan's change record are the evidence an auditor would ask for, so build them in from the first plan, not at audit time. This case names those standards; it does not teach them, and it makes no claim about any law on late pay.

recall.prompt: Your company's disaster recovery plan has passed its yearly tabletop exercise five years running. Last year's review listed "the recovery runbook still names the old database server; update it", with no name beside it. You've just been put in charge of the plan. What is the risk, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: An item with no owner and no due date doesn't get done; give each one a named owner and a date
A tabletop only talks; run a functional exercise that really does the risky step
The fix must change the plan's version and be checked by the next exercise

recall.model: The risk is that the plan says one thing and the systems another, and five tabletop passes can't show it, because a tabletop only talks: nobody follows the runbook against the real server. An item with no name beside it is a wish. I'd give that item, and every other open one, a named owner and a due date. When the runbook is fixed, the plan's version goes up, and the next exercise checks it: not another tabletop but a functional exercise that really restores the database at the second site from the runbook as written. I'd also call every contact and key holder in the plan each quarter.

recall.prompt: In the sim, keep a tabletop each March and every other setting as built. Which single change gets tonight's file to the bank with no day at all spent without an active key holder?
options: Calling everyone named in the plan every three months
Review items: an owner and a due date
recall.why: With an owner and a due date, R-7 is Ranulf's, due Monday 30 June 2025, and Aldegonde is enrolled that day, two months before Kisember leaves: 0 days without a key holder, and tonight's file goes at 04:06 after one dead number. The quarterly check finds Kisember gone on 30 September 2025, 60 days without; the monthly full-scale on 11 September 2025, 41 days without and 960 staff-hours a year; continuity software moves R-7 with no owner, and step 4 still fails at 03:16.

recall.prompt: According to NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, what should a full-scale functional exercise for a high-impact system include?
options: A discussion of roles round a table, with no equipment deployed
A system failover to the alternate location
A briefing on the plan's purpose and each person's role
A reading of the plan's phone numbers to check they look right
recall.why: The guide says: "The full-scale functional exercise should include a system failover to the alternate location." A discussion with no equipment is a tabletop, which "is discussion-based only and does not involve deploying equipment or other resources"; a briefing is training, not an exercise; and reading phone numbers is not calling them.

recall.prompt: In an interview you're asked: how would you run a continuity program for a company with many plans?

keyIdeas.idea: Every plan and every item has a named owner, with review dates and due dates
Exercises climb from talking it through to really doing one step, then everything
After-action reviews feed a lessons-learned loop that changes the plan and is checked by the next exercise
Contacts and key holders are checked every quarter, by calling them

recall.model: I'd run it as a program, not a pile of documents. Every plan has an owner and a review date, and its contacts and key holders are called every quarter, because people leave between exercises. Exercises climb a ladder: a tabletop to check roles and calls, then a functional exercise that really does the riskiest step, such as signing with a backup key at the second site, and now and then a full-scale exercise for the most important plans. After each exercise an after-action review lists what went wrong; each item gets an owner and a due date, the fix changes the plan and raises its version, and the next exercise checks it. I'd report two numbers each quarter: items past their due date, and steps never really run.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 6 months later. Every review item now has an owner and a due date, Aldegonde has been a key holder since Monday 16 November, the contacts are called each quarter, and on Thursday 11 March 2027 she signed a test file with the backup key at Ormsgill: PASS. The item list showed nothing open. One closed row was R-9, raised in November: "Ormsgill's copy is taken at 23:00, before Thursday's late timesheets arrive at 23:30; take it after 23:30." Its owner closed it on Friday 29 January 2027, the day she asked our IT supplier for the change. On Thursday 18 March 2027 the main storage failed again. All four steps worked and the file reached the bank before the cut-off, but Ormsgill's copy had been taken at 23:00 as always. The pay was worked out without the late timesheets, and their overtime was missing.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. R-9 was closed on time by its owner. Why did it still fail, and how should items be closed?

keyIdeas.idea: An item closed on its owner's word is not closed; close it only on evidence the change was made
The next exercise must really run the step each closed item touched; March's ran only step 4
Someone other than the owner checks the closure, and the plan's version records the change

coldCase.model: R-9 was closed on its owner's word, the day she asked for the change, not when the change was made and proven. Nobody looked at Ormsgill's copy time after that, and March's functional exercise really ran only step 4, signing a test file, so nothing would rerun step 3 and show the copy still came at 23:00. I'd close an item only on evidence: the change seen working, the plan's version raised to record it, and the step it touches really run in the next exercise. Every item closed since the last exercise goes on that exercise's list, and someone other than the owner checks it. And I'd rotate which step the yearly functional exercise really runs, so step 3 gets its turn.
